cases.evidence_note: p970 p. 19, Figuring the Credit, Example: joint return, dependent child in the junior (third) year, MAGI $70,000, qualified education expenses $4,300, "Jack and Kay can claim a $2,500 American opportunity credit in 2025. This is 100% of the first $2,000 of qualified education expenses, plus 25% of the next $2,000." Class A covers lines 27, 30, 1 and 7 ($4,000 and $2,500). The 40%/60% split (line 8 $1,000, line 9 and line 19 $1,500, Form 1040 line 29 $1,000) follows from the form, not the example; line 19 is $1,500 because the scaffolded tax exceeds it. Synthetic scaffolding (not in the example): the $70,000 MAGI is taxpayer W-2 wages; the child is 20, a full-time student, a qualifying child for the credit for other dependents only; all $4,300 is paid to the institution; "meet all of the requirements" is read as a 1098-T and EIN available, line 23 No, line 24 Yes, line 25 No (a junior has not completed 4 years), line 26 No.

p970 p. 28, Example: joint return, MAGI $75,000; Toni already has a bachelor's degree and paid $5,000 of qualified education expenses for the fall 2025 semester; "Bruce and Toni can claim a $1,000 (20% x $5,000) lifetime learning credit on their 2025 joint tax return." Class A covers lines 31, 10, 11, 12 and 18. Line 19 $1,000 follows because the tax exceeds it. The bachelor's degree is read as line 25 Yes (first 4 years completed before 2025), so the American opportunity credit is unavailable and lines 1 and 8 are zero. Synthetic scaffolding: Toni is the spouse entry; the $75,000 MAGI is taxpayer W-2 wages; the $5,000 is paid to the institution; Form 1098-T and EIN available; lines 23, 26 No, line 24 Yes.

p970 p. 20, Phaseout, Example: joint return, MAGI $165,000, $5,000 of qualified education expenses, tentative credit $2,500, ($180,000 - $165,000) / $20,000, "The result is the amount of your phased out (reduced) American opportunity credit ($1,875)." Class A covers lines 30, 1, 3, 4 and 7. Line 8 $750 and line 9 and line 19 $1,125 follow from the form (joint, so line 7 is refundable at 40%; the tax exceeds $1,125). The example does not say who the student is: the taxpayer is the student (adult, so the line 7 age test does not arise; joint in any case). Synthetic scaffolding: MAGI is taxpayer W-2 wages; the $5,000 is paid to the institution; Form 1098-T and EIN available; lines 23, 25, 26 No, line 24 Yes. The ratio 0.750 is exact, so the rounding ambiguity is not exercised.

p970 p. 29, Phaseout, Example: joint return, MAGI $161,000, $6,600 of qualified education expenses, "a $1,320 (20% x $6,600) tentative credit", ($180,000 - $161,000) / $20,000, "The result is the amount of your phased-out (reduced) lifetime learning credit ($1,254)." Class A covers lines 31, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15 and 18. Line 19 $1,254 follows because the tax exceeds it. The example does not name the student or say why the American opportunity credit is not used: the taxpayer is the student and has completed the first 4 years (line 25 Yes), so only the lifetime learning credit applies. Synthetic scaffolding: MAGI is taxpayer W-2 wages; the $6,600 is paid to the institution; Form 1098-T and EIN available. The ratio 0.950 is exact.

i8863 p. 5, Coordination with Pell grants, Example 1: $5,000 of qualified education expenses, a $5,000 Pell grant applied to them as a tax-free scholarship; "you will have $0 ($5,000 - $5,000) of adjusted qualified education expenses available to figure your credit. Your credit will be $0." Class A covers line 27 (worksheet line 2a $5,000) and the zero credit on lines 30, 1, 7, 8 and 19. Synthetic scaffolding (not in the example): the parent files single with $60,000 of W-2 wages; the child is 18, a full-time student and the parent's qualifying child (credit for other dependents only; no EIC at this income); the $5,000 is paid to the institution; "meet all other requirements" is read as Form 1098-T and EIN available, line 23 No, line 24 Yes, line 25 No (first semester), line 26 No. The parent is not the student; the parent is an adult born before 2002, answered for the Form 8863 line 7 test, which a non-joint filer is asked about themselves. The child's own return (the $4,000 included in the child's income) is not modeled.

i8863 p. 5, Example 2: only $1,000 of the Pell grant applied to qualified education expenses; "you will have $4,000 ($5,000 - $1,000) of adjusted qualified education expenses available to figure your credit. Your refundable American opportunity credit will be $1,000. Your nonrefundable credit may be as much as $1,500, but depends on your tax liability." Class A covers line 27 $4,000, line 8 and Form 1040 line 29 $1,000, and line 9 $1,500 (the "as much as" amount). Line 19 $1,500 is the scaffolded case where the tax exceeds $1,500. Synthetic scaffolding (not in the example): the parent files single with $60,000 of W-2 wages; the child is 18, a full-time student and the parent's qualifying child (credit for other dependents only; no EIC at this income); the $5,000 is paid to the institution; "meet all other requirements" is read as Form 1098-T and EIN available, line 23 No, line 24 Yes, line 25 No (first semester), line 26 No. The parent is not the student; the parent is an adult born before 2002, answered for the Form 8863 line 7 test, which a non-joint filer is asked about themselves. The child's own return (the $4,000 included in the child's income) is not modeled.

i8863 p. 5, Example 2, last sentence: "If you're not otherwise required to file a tax return, you should file to get a refund of your $1,000 refundable credit, but your tax liability and nonrefundable credit will be $0." Class A covers line 8, Form 1040 line 29 and the $1,000 refund (lines 33, 34), line 19 $0 and line 22 $0. Line 9 $1,500 follows from the form. The "not otherwise required to file" parent is scaffolded with no income at all (no W-2), single, claiming the 18-year-old student child; the other scaffolding is as in pell.ex2.

p970 p. 15, Example 1, no scholarship: AGI and MAGI $39,250, standard deduction $15,750, "taxable income of $23,500 and an income tax liability before credits of $2,585", "qualified education expenses of $4,000, which results in a credit of $2,500 and a tax liability after credits of $85 ($2,585 - $2,500)." Class A covers lines 11b, 15, 16, 27 and 7; lines 8 $1,000, 19 $1,500, 22 and 24 $1,085 and 29 $1,000 follow from the form and are the form reading of the $85 (line 24 $1,085 less line 29 $1,000). No EIC at this AGI. Bill is 28, unmarried (single), first-year full-time student in a degree program; "Bill and the college meet all the requirements" is read as Form 1098-T and EIN available, line 23 No, line 24 Yes, line 25 No, line 26 No; born before 2002, so the line 7 refundability test does not apply. Synthetic scaffolding: the AGI the example states without a source is W-2 wages with no withholding; the $5,600 of qualified education expenses is paid to the institution (room and board are excluded and not entered). The publication's "tax liability after credits" nets the $1,000 refundable credit (Form 1040 line 29) against the tax; on the form the nonrefundable $1,500 reduces line 22 and the $1,000 is a payment.

p970 pp. 15-16, Example 2, scholarship excluded from income: a $5,600 scholarship usable for any expense, excluded from income; "Bill's adjusted qualified education expenses would be zero, and there would be no education credit. Therefore, Bill's tax liability after credits would be $2,585." Class A covers line 27 $0 (worksheet line 2a $5,600), lines 7 and 19 $0, and lines 16, 22 and 24 $2,585. The scholarship does not exceed the period's expenses (line 2a equals line 1). Bill is 28, unmarried (single), first-year full-time student in a degree program; "Bill and the college meet all the requirements" is read as Form 1098-T and EIN available, line 23 No, line 24 Yes, line 25 No, line 26 No; born before 2002, so the line 7 refundability test does not apply. The publication's "tax liability after credits" nets the $1,000 refundable credit (Form 1040 line 29) against the tax; on the form the nonrefundable $1,500 reduces line 22 and the $1,000 is a payment.

p970 p. 16, Example 3, scholarship partially included in income: $4,000 of the $5,600 scholarship included in income (Schedule 1 line 8r) and deemed applied to room and board; the remaining $1,600 reduces expenses (worksheet line 2a); "the adjusted qualified education expenses would be $4,000. Bill's AGI and MAGI would increase to $43,250, the taxable income would increase to $27,500, and the tax liability before credits would increase to $3,065", credit $2,500, "the tax liability after credits would be $565 ($3,065 - $2,500)." Class A covers lines 8r, 11b, 15, 16, 27 and 7; lines 8 $1,000, 19 $1,500, 22 and 24 $1,565 and 29 $1,000 are the form reading of the $565. Example 4 (the scholarship paid directly to the college) has the same inputs and results and is not a separate case. Bill is 28, unmarried (single), first-year full-time student in a degree program; "Bill and the college meet all the requirements" is read as Form 1098-T and EIN available, line 23 No, line 24 Yes, line 25 No, line 26 No; born before 2002, so the line 7 refundability test does not apply. p970 p. 16, Example 5, scholarship excluded: "The AGI and MAGI would be $24,125. The tax liability before any credits would be $51. The qualified education expenses would be reduced to $500. Jane would be able to receive a $251 American opportunity credit ($200 refundable and $51 nonrefundable), a $1,700 additional child tax credit, and a $4,204 EIC. In total, Jane would be able to receive a tax refund of $6,104." Class A covers lines 11b, 16, 27, 8, 19, 29, 28, 27a and 33/34. Line 7 $500 and line 22 $0 follow (the $51 tax is fully offset, so the nonrefundable child tax credit is zero and the whole $1,700 is refundable). Worksheet line 2a $5,500, Schedule 1 line 8r $0. Jane is 28, unmarried, files head of household with her 10-year-old qualifying child (EIC and child tax credit), first-year full-time certificate student; wages $24,125 on a W-2 with no withholding and no other income or adjustments, except the scholarship she includes in income, entered on Schedule 1 line 8r. "Jane and the college meet all the requirements" is read as Form 1098-T and EIN available, line 23 No, line 24 Yes, line 25 No, line 26 No; born before 2002, so the line 7 refundability test does not apply. Synthetic scaffolding: head of household (the example says unmarried with a dependent child; household.home_cost Yes); the $6,000 is paid to the institution; the scholarship allocated to tuition does not exceed the period's expenses. The publication's "American opportunity credit" total is the allowed amount: Form 8863 line 8 (refundable) plus line 19 (nonrefundable, limited by the tax).

Stage 15 return H1 (married filing jointly, one child aged 4, expenses $6,000, plan maximum $5,000) with the $5,000 of W-2 box 10 moved to the spouse: you wages $3,000 and no box 10; spouse wages $40,000 and box 10 $5,000 (none in box 1). Part III by hand from i2441: line 12 $5,000; 16 $6,000; 17 $5,000; 18 $3,000 and 19 $40,000 ("earned income doesn't include any dependent care benefits shown on line 12"); 20 $3,000; 21 $5,000; 22 $0; 23 $5,000; 24 $0; 25 $3,000; 26 $2,000 (to Form 1040 line 1e); 27 $3,000; 28 $3,000; 29 $0, so line 31 is $0 and no credit remains. Lines 4 and 5: "If filing jointly, figure your and your spouse's earned income separately" and earned income includes "The amount shown on Form 1040 ... line 1z"; under the owner ruling amb.2025.dc_line1e_attribution line 1e is the earned income of the spouse whose Forms W-2 show box 10 (only the spouse here): line 4 = $3,000, line 5 = $40,000 + $2,000 = $42,000.
